national.title: Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa
national.summary: South Africa is working to overcome a children's literacy crisis. In one Johannesburg township, a reading club is instilling a love of books in kids — and inspiring them to become authors.
national.body:
Fiona Mogane, 13, contributed the story "Lindani's Modelling Journey" to From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex, a new book of short stories written by kids who are part of the "Read Alex" literacy program in Johannesburg. Participants in weekly classes wrote stories drawing on their own lives. Madalene Cronje for NPR hide caption

JOHANNESBURG — It's an ordinary Saturday morning in Alexandra township, known simply as Alex or sometimes dubbed Gomora, a reference to the biblical city of Gomorrah that was known for its wickedness.

That nickname stems from Alexandra's high crime rates. It's a high-density area, where tin shacks stretch as far as the eye can see and rotting garbage piles up along potholed streets.

But that image doesn't intrude on an event at a small building at the Kwabhekilanga Sports Ground. There's a palpable sense of excitement. Something different is happening this weekend and community members have turned up for it.

It's a book launch for a collection entitled From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex . The seven stories in the self-published anthology have been written by children from the township who attend a free weekly literacy program.

South Africa is in the midst of a literacy crisis, with one international study showing a majority of 10-year-olds — some 81% — are unable to read for meaning in any of South Africa's 12 official languages.

Sandton, widely known as Africa's richest square mile, can be seen in the distance, only a few miles from Alexandra township. Madelene Cronjé/Madelene Cronjé/NPR hide caption

The grassroots program Read Alex has been trying to change this, offering a weekend reading club, mainly in English, to instill a love of books in children. Launched by the Run Alex Athletics Club, it has about 50 participants. Among the activities: an annual public speaking competition, two spelling bees and a book drive on Mandela Day every year that brings in about 500 volumes — some of which the kids take home and some of which go to libraries.

national.title: French activists demand a tear gas suspension over reported menstrual changes
national.summary: Some women reported painful cramps, unexpected bleeding and disrupted menstrual cycles after exposure, and an advocacy group says it has collected more than 10,000 complaints.
national.body:
Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press

PARIS (AP) — French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent street protests that authorities suspend the use of tear gas to disperse crowds over concerns it's caused menstrual changes and other reproductive health problems, though scientists have not confirmed a medical connection.

WATCH: Why French students are leading massive protests across the country

The demands come after police used tear gas during student protests and demonstrations over the cost of living, some marred by violence. Some women reported painful cramps, unexpected bleeding and disrupted menstrual cycles after exposure, and an advocacy group says it has collected more than 10,000 complaints. Opposition lawmakers are seeking a ban and independent research into possible health effects.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has rejected the calls, saying police use of tear gas is essential to crowd control as an alternative to using more dangerous weapons.

Here's what is known — and what is not — about tear gas and reproductive health.

Tear gas grenades used by French police contain CS, a chemical irritant that affects the eyes, skin and respiratory tract. CS is a crystalline powder dispersed into the air as fine particles. Its effects depend upon how much is used and how long people are exposed to it.

Those exposed during the protests include peaceful demonstrators — including children, pregnant women and older people — and residents near the sites of protest marches.

national.title: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
national.summary: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone strike on Saturday. Kyiv has yet to comment.
national.body:
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.

The the Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.

It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.

The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

national.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
national.summary: Libya's eastern government says the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia.
national.body:
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.

The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.

It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

national.title: As AI detects flaws in computer systems, is it causing more tech outages and disruptions?
national.summary: AI rapidly identifies computer system vulnerabilities and companies are pressured to fix them. Experts say that might lead to unintended consequences, like tech outages.
national.body:
In the span of one week, Microsoft services went down, flights were grounded nationwide, some banks' services briefly stopped working and an internal platform for the National Security Agency went dark.

It left people wondering: Is artificial intelligence the culprit?

In a Fox News interview, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he asked someone in the tech industry what could be causing the outages, and that person believed it's "super intelligence," the Trump administration's preferred term for AI (they're not the same thing).

"That kinda makes sense to me, because I can tell you with 98% certainty, we're not seeing the cyberattack, no one's out there taking claims for it," Mullin said Nov 17.

WATCH: Mounting tech disruptions raise concerns about U.S. cybersecurity

In a separate Nov. 17 Fox Business interview, National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton pointed to flaws that AI detected in a programming language used in systems across the world, and he said fixing them caused unexpected problems.

"The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected. That is what has happened at the NSA today," he said.

Senate Intelligence Committee Vice Chairman Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said some of the recent outages were "AI-related."

national.title: Mercury gets its first visitor in years as a pair of spacecraft loop into orbit
national.summary: BepiColombo is only the third spacecraft to visit Mercury — the sun's closest planet and barely bigger than our moon — and the first in more than a decade.
national.body:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — A pair of spacecraft slipped into orbit around Mercury on Saturday after an eight-year cruise through the inner solar system to unravel our littlest planet's mountain of mysteries.

The linked robotic explorers — one European, the other Japanese — will separate from one another next month in order to map and study the scorching little planet from different altitudes. The $2 billion (1.7 billion euros) mission is known collectively as BepiColombo.

The European Space Agency announced BepiColombo's arrival via social media. A series of thruster firings slowed the spacecraft enough to be captured by the planet's weak gravity. But it took several anxious hours before flight controllers in Germany — 94 million miles (152 million kilometers) away — could confirm that BepiColombo had achieved orbit. Teams pored over the data streaming back; additional information was not immediately available.

BepiColombo is only the third spacecraft to visit Mercury — the sun's closest planet and barely bigger than our moon — and the first in more than a decade.

NASA's Mariner 10 flew past Mercury three times in the mid-1970s. The team included the late Italian mathematician Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo, for whom this latest mission is named. NASA's Messenger spacecraft entered orbit around Mercury in 2011 and, after running out of fuel, crashed into the planet in 2015.

Launched in 2018, BepiColombo took a slower, more roundabout route to get to Mercury, flying once past Earth, twice past Venus and six times past Mercury for gravity-guiding assists. All those loop-de-loops put more than 6 billion miles (10 billion kilometers) on the odometer. The conjoined spacecraft shed their mother ship in September for the final leg of the journey.

WATCH: Astronauts reflect on living aboard the International Space Station

Lead project scientist Geraint Jones said he and others can't wait for all the new data to start streaming down in the spring. The mission will provide the ability to compare "unprecedented measurements taken by two spacecraft at the planet at the same time," he noted.

national.title: Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels
national.summary: Some 200 countries gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual climate negotiations. Countries failed to reach an agreement over fossil fuels - the primary driver of global warming.
national.body:
COP31 President Murat Kurum, center, leaves a closing plenary session at the U.N. Climate Summit, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from fossil fuels like coal and natural gas. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption

ANTALYA, Turkey — International climate change talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels. On Sunday, nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas.

The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions .

After representatives of the EU walked out, other countries also objected – including Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands.

The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."

This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been scientific consensus that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.

Negotiations at this year's U.N. Climate Summit were supposed to end Friday but there was no agreement on language about fossil fuels. Activists demonstrated by holding signs that read "shame" at COP31, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption

Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts , like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035 . That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.

national.title: UN climate talks break down over bitter disagreements on fossil fuels
national.summary: Expectations had already been low heading into the two-week negotiations in Turkey, but impasses over explicitly including fossil fuels and other issues, including money, proved irreconcilable.
national.body:
Suzan Fraser, Associated Press Suzan Fraser, Associated Press

Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Seth Borenstein, Associated Press

Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press

ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — United Nations climate talks couldn't reach an overarching agreement on Sunday because of disagreements over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming.

Expectations had already been low heading into the two-week negotiations in Turkey, but impasses over explicitly including fossil fuels and other issues, including money, proved irreconcilable.

Though the talks, called COP31, failed to reach a main agreement known as a cover decision, the meeting had already made progress on smaller issues.

This all happened as global warming accelerates with ever-worsening heat waves, floods, storms and droughts. The U.N. said it is now inevitable that the world will soon blow past the warming threshold established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement. And there is also a global energy shock due to the war in Iran. On top of that, a strong El Niño amplifies human-caused warming and causes more weather disasters.

Any pact approved at the talks requires near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they could not accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership, which didn't mention fossil fuels. A considerably larger number of nations accepted the decision, often reluctantly, saying consensus on something was more important, though it ultimately failed. Russia and Saudi Arabia sought to keep fossil fuels out of the document.

Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.

Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who "overstayed his visa in violation of our nation's laws."

During the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers," the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."

Environmental groups had filed lawsuits on Thursday to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.

The detonation, originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, was paused after a federal court order. The Army now plans to act by 24 November.

The federal court suspended the detonation on Friday after residents of Middletown, Iowa expressed concern over the risk of toxic lead particles spreading across the surrounding area.

In the new filing late on Saturday evening, the Department of the Army said it planned to invoke an emergency exclusion to skirt a court-issued pause.

It argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.

national.body: COP31, the United Nations' annual climate conference, ended Sunday without a final agreement after days of contentious talks collapsed, mainly because of disputes between nations pushing to phase out fossil fuel use and others opposed to doing so.The breakdown capped two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, between delegations from nearly 200 countries. Their debates ran into overtime, becoming the longest COP summit in history, at a moment that U.N. officials and many scientists have called decisive for the trajectory of global warming and climate change.U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said in a statement that Sunday he was "deeply disappointed" by the outcome of the summit."I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," he said. "But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science."The United States sent no representatives to the climate conference for the second year in a row, following the Trump administration's withdrawal from the 2015 Paris Agreement. national.body:
At least three people have been killed after a fire at a confectionery factory in western Java on Saturday, with the death toll expected to rise.

Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for around 36 missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.

Rescuers recovered 24 body bags from the fire as of Sunday evening, as search operations continue to locate missing people.

Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.

The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.

Local media reported that the search had been called off for the night late on Sunday, and would resume on Monday.

"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.

national.title: Medicare looks a bit different in 2027, so don't miss open enrollment
national.summary: Open enrollment for Medicare runs through Dec. 7, and there are a few different pitfalls people should watch out for this year. Your drug plan or Medicare Advantage plan could be changing a lot.
national.body:
Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people . The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.

Open enrollment runs through Dec. 7. The plan you choose takes effect on Jan. 1, for the full calendar year.

Health Policy Is your Medicare Advantage plan ending next year? Here's what to know Build-your-own Medicare menu Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn't one plan. It's more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.

Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there's no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn't cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.

As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D , the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.

This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.

"People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs," said David Lipschutz , a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.

Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It's a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can't find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.

national.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
national.summary: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.
national.body:
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.

He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.

The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.

"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.

"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.

The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.

national.title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
national.summary: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".
national.body:
Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.

His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.

Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.

The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".

The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.

Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.

national.title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
national.summary: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.
national.body:
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.

Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores, the secretariat continued.

national.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
national.summary: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
national.body:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.

The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.

It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

When asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.

"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," Trump added.

This apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyber-attacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with Trump saying he was not good enough.

Dan Lorhmann, a former analyst for the National Security Agency (NSA), told the BBC News Channel that the NCIC's data included "critical information relating to nationwide criminal activity" and needed to be protected.

national.body:
Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.

At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.

He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.

"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.

But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.

Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.

The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.

His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.

national.title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
national.summary: When 16-year-old Landon Tresp met a teenage girl in an online game, it led to him and his mother helping the FBI rescue her from kidnapping.
national.body:
Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.

She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.

He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.

Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.

That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight.

"She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.

The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.

Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue.

national.title: Why do people believe recent tech failures must be connected?
national.summary: Even without clear evidence, people drew connections between recent tech failures and outages. The way our brains and social media platforms work helps explain why.
national.body:
Companies including Microsoft, United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase and U.S. Bank experienced technical issues and outages that caused widespread banking issues, delayed plane departures and interrupted workdays across the world. Soon after, Marriott and Apple customers also experienced digital problems, and 178 companies reported being affected by a Nov. 16 cyberattack.

At the same time, various U.S. government systems — the Federal Aviation Administration, National Security Agency and National Weather Service — fell into disarray, including a rare nationwide ground stop. For many people, the pile-on of concerning news alerts had a sinister feel.

WATCH: Mounting tech disruptions raise concerns about U.S. cybersecurity

"We're under attack in a way we've never seen before," wrote Nalin Haley, a conservative influencer and son of Republican politician Nikki Haley, on Nov. 17. "This is an AI cyberattack."

On Bluesky, Christopher Webb, a self-described "lifelong Dem" and party strategist, questioned whether the issues were connected.

"Coincidence??? 4 major banks reporting outages, a massive Microsoft disruption, and a nationwide FAA ground stop, all within days of each other," he wrote Nov. 16.

The best available information points to mundane explanations such as routine maintenance, one-off problems or isolated cyberattacks, rather than an imminent systemic collapse or a coordinated attack on digital systems.

The rapid-fire succession of events didn't help. Neither did the timing of a planned, routine Nov. 17 test of the country's Emergency Alert System.

national.title: For families of the fallen, Trump's proposed arch casts a shadow over Arlington National Cemetery
national.summary: Trump's proposed 250-foot-tall arch could cast a long shadow on Arlington National Cemetery, with the potential to literally shade gravesites, disrupt solemn visits with the noise of construction and alter the carefully designed historic landscape of the nation's capital.
national.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Cpl. Spencer Collart's headstone faces the rising sun and the Lincoln Memorial to the east. The Marine Corps War Memorial is nearby. Soon, President Donald Trump's gilded, towering arch could be, too.

Collart's silent stone speaks volumes in its simplicity of courage, sacrifice and loss. It stands among thousands of uniform headstones and other monuments, each telling the story of the person, or persons, beneath it.

WATCH: 2nd judge blocks construction of Trump's arch in D.C.

But if Trump gets his way, a different story may be told. His proposed 250-foot-tall (76-meter-tall) arch could cast a long shadow on Arlington National Cemetery, with the potential to literally shade gravesites, disrupt solemn visits with the noise of construction and alter the carefully designed historic landscape of the nation's capital.

For many veterans and their families, and the loved ones of others buried at the cemetery, the arch has no place so close to the Arlington, Virginia, burial grounds. That opposition has sparked lawsuits by veterans groups and others, including nine family members of the Kennedy political dynasty, who argue the arch, which would be built on a traffic circle about half a mile (0.8 kilometers) from Arlington's main entrance, will fundamentally change the experience of visiting the cemetery.

"It's a billboard for an ego. It's a loud, boastful, gaudy piece of marketing dropped onto sacred ground," said Bart Collart, Spencer's father. His son, a young Marine who died at 21 trying to save fellow crew members in a 2023 Osprey crash in Australia, would see it as "dirtying hallowed ground."

The arch project is part of a series of renovations to Washington that Trump, a Republican, has set in motion to reimagine the city. When complete, the gold and granite arch will stretch taller than the Lincoln Memorial.

Opponents say the arch would break the alignment between the Lincoln Memorial, the Memorial Bridge and Arlington House, which was formerly Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee's home, and the symbolism of a reunited North and South.

national.title: Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress
national.summary: President Trump is directing federal contractors to consult the White House about inquiries from Congress and to withhold any communications that his administration considers privileged.
national.body:
President Trump speaks at a news conference in the James Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington. Jacquelyn Martin/AP hide caption

NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order .

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

The order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets , noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon.

White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations initiated by Democrats.

Trump's counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that they must seek approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality."

Garcia sent letters this week directing members of Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

Responding to the new executive order, Garcia said it was part of the administration's "blatant attack on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight." He said that despite efforts to impede investigations, "we're just getting started."

national.title: Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000
national.summary: The hair was given as a sign of friendship shortly before Washington's death in 1799, according to a descendent of its former owner.
national.body:
A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (£3,058).

The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.

Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.

Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.

McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".

Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.

Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.

Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.

Duvall then intentionally and knowingly spit in the face of an officer during the course of the stop. Officers then took Duvall into custody following a brief struggle.

Sienna M. Swanson, 33, then facilitated the movement of vehicle that was stopped for a violation. Swanson was taken into custody without incident. Later during the course of the traffic stop, Travis Goodlow, 24, did get into the suspect vehicle and moved the vehicle. Goodlow was subsequently taken into custody without incident. local.body:
The Mental Health Association in Chautauqua County (MHA) November recovery luncheon was not only an opportunity to recognize participants for their accomplishments but to express gratitude to staff and volunteers for their service.

As they have for several years, Bonnie Weber, of Be The Change You Want to See in Jamestown, and her volunteers again prepared and served a delicious dinner at the MHA's Thanksgiving luncheon. Working with her were George Brightman, John Case, Shannon Ramirez, and Bill Schmidt. Jon Bogue offered grace.

Among those receiving certificates for their progress were three participants who completed Strong Foundations, an intense 15-week program, using encouragement, practical tools, and community for single parents to build strong, faith-filled homes.

Weber presented roses not only to the participants but to staff as well, in appreciation of their work and commitment. She also recognized volunteers and community supporters, including John Felton, CEO at the Southern Chautauqua Federal Credit Union.

All are encouraged to mark their calendars now for the MHA's second annual fundraiser at the Frewsburg American Legion on Saturday, February 27. Admission will be free, with basket and gift card raffles, a 50/50 drawing, live music, and food and beverages available for purchase.

The Mental Health Association in Chautauqua County is a peer recovery center offering support groups and individual coaching for people looking to improve their lives, deepen wellness, thrive in recovery, or support those on a recovery path. Peers use their personal stories to help people find recovery in their own lives in their own way.

The Jamestown center is at Door 14 in the rear of the Gateway Center, 31 Water Street. Hours are 9:30 a.m.-4:30 p.m. Monday-Thursday and 9 a.m.-4 p.m. Fridays.

The North County recovery center is open Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays, 9:30 a.m.-4 p.m. in Grace Lutheran Church at 601 Eagle Street in Dunkirk.

local.title: Healing with Horses: Birthday visit can be memorable experience
local.summary: Every parent wants their children to know how special they are. When better to celebrate than on their birthday. When my kids started to go to school (in the 1980s), I discovered birthday parties. When it was my daughter’s birthday, I did the mom thing and had a party and she invited her friends, an
local.body:
Every parent wants their children to know how special they are. When better to celebrate than on their birthday.

When my kids started to go to school (in the 1980s), I discovered birthday parties. When it was my daughter's birthday, I did the mom thing and had a party and she invited her friends, and they came. When it was my son's birthday, I tried the same thing, but only one little boy came. It was the boy who was constantly bullied at school. To be his friend meant you were also bullied, but I didn't know any of that then.

Real friendships are built on common bonds and interests, and ultimately, what you get out of a relationship. Who are the friends of children who are different? And when do people really put the feelings of others above themselves?

Today birthday parties can be very creative, and expensive, including taking the party to places outside of the home. It is important to have friends and feel like you belong to a "social" group, but what does it take to make your child feel special these days? And not just that one day, but everyday. I love the "Winnie the Pooh" story of the "unbirthday" celebrations. Then there are 364 days to celebrate with friends instead of just one day. And Eeyore was always included.

But let's go back to the problem of nobody showing up to your party.

Centaur Stride has a program policy to help people make friends and feel special even on their unbirthdays. Friendships and relationships are built on common ground. What does a child with a disability or who is different, neurodivergent or other, have in common with their classmates, cousins or neighborhood kids that is enough to make a bond? One where you have something to talk about, laugh about or just share an experience?

Who doesn't want to go horseback riding? At Centaur Stride, it is definitely not something where social status matters. Our "Friends and Family" program allows a rider to share their lesson with a friend or family member at no additional expense. They can groom a horse together and share ride time. (Instructors must know in advance and all paperwork must be filled out and signed by the participant’s parent.) Would someone say no to a personal invitation like that? During the experience, they can talk about the horse, bond with the horse, and use the horse as a link therapist to bridge a common interest (the horse). Afterwards, in school, at home or in the community, they have a shared experience to talk about on a deeper level than just saying hi. Others who overhear the conversation also usually take an interest and ask questions.

local.title: Little Mice by Dunkirk’s Caleb Spell
Seeking a peace, even for modern-day monsters
local.summary: Like many boys growing up in the 1950s and ‘60s, I was fascinated by monsters. My prized possessions were models of classic horror figures. The stories behind them were thrilling — the battle of the giants King Kong and Godzilla, the rag-clad mummy brought back to life from ancient Egypt, and the ha
local.body:
Like many boys growing up in the 1950s and '60s, I was fascinated by monsters. My prized possessions were models of classic horror figures. The stories behind them were thrilling -- the battle of the giants King Kong and Godzilla, the rag-clad mummy brought back to life from ancient Egypt, and the half-fish, half-man Creature who dwelled in the depths of the Black Lagoon.

Of course I outgrew the toys, but my fascination with malformations of nature never disappeared. There are three classic monster figures which, sixty years later, continue to be a source of dark intrigue for me, mainly because of what they tell us about the nature of man.

As a kid, I favored the Wolfman, in part because I loved dogs. If I was to choose my monster self, it would have been that hairy, agile, dog-like beast who howled at the moon. Later, I began to understand the deeper meaning. The wolfman revealed the violent nature that lurks in our subconscious. As a matter of philosophy, it is a reminder of the need for a social contract (laws) because the threat of violence is always there, just beneath the surface. As a matter of psychology, it echoes Freud's theory of the human psyche (the Id). It is, in short, the Beast Within.

During the '80s and '90s, Bram Stoker's original "Dracula" evolved from sheer grotesque barbarism to assume dark, sado-masochistic qualities. The nature of his evil became refined, sexualized, primed for commercial success. Yet, despite sensationalized Dracula sequels, the themes remain intact. It's essentially about the struggle of good versus evil in the context of Christianity and the Holy Cross.

I was teaching a high school AP literature class when I first took on Mary Shelley's "Frankenstein," perhaps the most challenging novel I've ever read. This is a story that explores the most complex and disturbing aspects of the human condition.

On a dreary November evening, Victor Frankenstein, the obsessed philosopher/scientist, brings to life his creation -- a human-like creature cobbled together with body parts stolen from the graveyard. Victor has created life from the unliving. In so doing, he assumes the role of God. With that role might have come a responsibility, like that of a father to his son -- a sense of duty to protect and provide for. Instead, Victor Frankenstein is overcome with dread and disgust. He abandons his child.

Frankenstein, the monster, enters the world without a name, without family or guidance. In pursuit of his Maker, he acts out, killing Victor's brother and fleeing into the wilderness. Hiding there, he comes upon the simple home of a happy family led by a blind father. During this time, his only period of peace, he spies on the family and learns of the virtues of life and love. Yet his serenity is short-lived, as the family discovers his wretched appearance and drives him back into the woods. His recourse would be revenge, the burning down of the house of love.

Main cast seniors gather backstage after wrapping the closing performance of Clue: High School Edition. From left to right: Eliza Pound (Ms. Scarlet), Bella DeGolier (Mrs. Peacock), JJ Whipple (Professor Plum), Mallory Berndt (Mrs. White), Richard Kuras (Wadsworth).

GOWANDA -- The Gowanda High School Thespian Society successfully wrapped up its production of "Clue: High School Edition" earlier this month, completing a three-show run that delivered a high-energy, campy murder mystery to enthusiastic community audiences.

The production transformed the high school auditorium into Boddy Manor through an innovative moveable set conceived by director Ms. K. Merrill, a student teacher who joined longtime producer Mrs. Nobles to lead the show. Building the iconic rooms -- including the Study, Library, Kitchen, Hall, and Billiards Room -- was a collaborative effort involving the entire cast and crew, led by Garry Smith (Head of Construction and Stage Manager) who brought Boddy Manor from just a concept to the reality of Gowanda's auditorium stage. Beyond the ingenious set design, student actors and crew members executed the fast-paced comedy with sharp, clever timing and detailed staging.

Merrill and Nobles guided the production from concept to curtain call, overseeing set construction, character development, and wardrobe design. Senior actors and leads Mallory Berndt (Mrs. White) and Eliza Pound (Ms. Scarlet) stepped up as Costume Co-Captains, helping their fellow cast members build unique costumes, select props, and develop distinct stage personalities.

Following last fall's production of Knock Knock, the directors sought a title tailored to the talents of their ensemble.

“We have returning students who are instinctively funny, so we wanted something a little more grown-up and witty,” said Merrill.

The final curtain call honored the district’s graduating seniors, marking their final fall play performance on the Gowanda High School stage: Eliza Pound (Ms. Scarlet); Bella DeGolier (Mrs. Peacock); JJ Whipple (Professor Plum); Mallory Berndt (Mrs. White); Richard Kuras (Wadsworth); Amelia Pickering (Sound); Molly Booth (Sound).

local.title: Small pick-up can almost always change a life
local.summary: The call came into the principal’s office a few minutes after 8 a.m. I had completed the daily announcements, done my morning walkabout and checked in with a few needy kids. I was just about to sit down to answer some emails and complete some paperwork when the direct line to my office rang. I […]
local.body:
The call came into the principal's office a few minutes after 8 a.m. I had completed the daily announcements, done my morning walkabout and checked in with a few needy kids.

I was just about to sit down to answer some emails and complete some paperwork when the direct line to my office rang. I recognized the stressed voice on the other end of the line immediately. It was the voice of a woman who had been a student in my math class more than 20 years prior.

She had her troubles growing up and she had given me a run for my money as a student. But I liked her very much. I never took students' misbehavior personally, no matter how insulting, disrespectful or frustrating. And I have never held a kid's missteps against them years later. Who is the same person that they were in middle school? A good educator has to be able to love the unlovable and to have a bottomless well of forgiveness. Anyone lacking in these areas has no business working with kids.

This former student was now struggling as a single mom to raise two spirited daughters of her own. We had communicated numerous times while I worked with this parent as she tried to bring her girls under control. She would tell me that she considered her child rearing struggles as payback for the hell she gave her parents and teachers. And I would chuckle and tell her that she wasn't that bad and neither were her girls.

Mom was having an especially difficult time getting her youngest to come to school. Like many parents, mom had to be at work before her kids got on the bus. And her long work day ended well after school let out.

Her sixth-grade daughter would often pretend to get ready for school, say goodbye to her mother when she left for work and then just stay at home. Other times she would ride the bus to school but instead of entering the building she would walk away and find a place to hang out for the day. Sometimes she would play hooky with a friend at an unsupervised household. On a few occasions daughter was found hanging out at Walmart, McDonald's and other establishments near school grounds. In an effort to get her daughter to school, mom changed her work schedule and started driving her daughter to school.

On this particular morning, my former student was calling from the school drop-off. Her little darling was refusing to get out of the car and come into the building. Mom asked if I could come out to her vehicle and help convince her daughter to come into school. Of course I said yes.

entertainment.title: Rings Of Power: What Is The Secret Fire In The Lord Of The Rings?
entertainment.summary: Season 3, Episode 3 of The Rings of Power is called The Secret Fire. Here's what we know about this mysterious force based on J.R.R. Tolkien's writings.
entertainment.body:
Ben Rothstein/Prime Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Contains spoilers for "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 3 — "The Secret Fire."

In "The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 3 , Tolkien's Secret Fire is not simply referenced, but it is a present character. (Heck, the episode is even named after it.) So what is this mysterious glowing force with Moses-and-the-burning-bush vibes? While Tolkien stays cryptic about the specifics in his writings, it isn't a stretch to say that the Secret Fire is God himself — at least, kind of. It's confusing.

In the episode, Gandalf discovers a mysterious flame in the deserts of Rhûn. It doesn't burn him when he touches it — and when he calls it the Secret Fire, it responds with a voice, saying, "You know me not. I am that which burns within all things yet still remains unseen. I built the heavens and stars, and all of Middle-earth is cradled within my flame." It goes on to explain the history of the Wizards, one of whom was already killed off-screen . That answers one burning question fans had going into the new season. But what about the mysterious flame itself? It's described as endless — and it is. It's been around since before Middle-earth was shaped or the universe (which Tolkien calls Eä) came into being.

The book "The Silmarillion" introduces the Secret Fire by saying, "Therefore Ilúvatar gave to their vision Being, and set it amid the Void, and the Secret Fire was sent to burn at the heart of the World; and it was called Eä." There's a lot to unpack there. Let's break it down.

Prime Video The Secret Fire is also called the Flame Imperishable and the Imperishable Flame. It first comes up when Tolkien's version of the One God, which he calls Eru Ilúvatar, creates the universe. He does this by composing an epic musical score with his angels (some of whom afterward become the god-like protectors of Middle-earth called the Valar and Maiar). When they finish their song, we get the line we already saw introducing the Secret Fire. Ilúvatar turns the music into a vision and then gives that vision Being. Then he uses the Secret Fire as the central life-giving force at the center of the world.

The tricky part about the Secret Fire is its relationship to the Creator. Tolkien can be really enigmatic when it comes to magical elements in his world. That's why the way the Rings of Power work in Prime Video's series differs from in the "Lord of the Rings" books , for instance. In the case of the Secret Fire, Tolkien doesn't make the relationship between the Fire and Ilúvatar definitively clear. Instead, Ilúvatar is referenced as the Creator being, whereas the Secret Fire is seen more as an element or manifestation of his power.

entertainment.title: Tom Jackson, Denver Broncos’ All-Pro Linebacker and ESPN Analyst, Dies at 75
entertainment.summary: He spent nearly 30 years with the network, often teaming with Chris Berman: “We’ve lost one of the best human beings ever to walk the planet.”
entertainment.body:
Tom Jackson, who parlayed a 14-season stint as a stalwart linebacker on the Denver Broncos’ famed “Orange Crush” defense into a long career as a popular football analyst on ESPN , has died. He was 75.

Jackson died Friday, his family told the network. No cause was announced.

Jackson was best known for his work alongside Chris Berman on the ESPN shows NFL Primetime and Sunday NFL Countdown , where the pair would deliver their humorous, entertaining take on highlights from games. Related Stories Music Peak Halftime Show: The A-List Machine Eventizing Pro Games Movies Lance Broadway, Pitcher Turned 'Olympus Has Fallen' Actor, Dies at 43

“All of us are stunned,” Berman said in a statement. “I’m stunned, we’re stunned and you’re stunned. We’ve lost one of the best human beings ever to walk the planet, Tom Jackson. I was fortunate to work side by side with Tom for 30 years … It was a labor of love for our whole team, both in front of the camera and behind it. We always hoped our viewers enjoyed the shows as much as we did bringing it to them every week.”

Berman said on Sunday NFL Countdown that Jackson’s death was unexpected and that he had spoken with his best friend “at length” on Tuesday. “He was a vital 75,” he said.

“Tom was so much more than an accomplished NFL analyst,” he said in his statement. “There was nobody kinder, more thoughtful, more loyal or more engaging than him. And when it came to laughter, Tom’s was frequent and unmistakable. He is easily summed up by this classic old song: ‘He’s got sunshine on a cloudy day.’”

Added ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro, “He brought the credibility of an All-Pro NFL player, the insight of a gifted analyst and a warmth and authenticity that connected with generations of football fans.”

ESPN’s NFL studio is named the Chris Berman-Tom Jackson Studio.

entertainment.title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Slays $120M at Box Office as Franchise Heats Back Up
entertainment.summary: The sixth film in the Lionsgate series rebounded after 2023's 'The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes,' while freshly expanded 'I Play Rocky' and newcomer 'Elsinore' also came out swinging.
entertainment.body:
Logo text The Hunger Games franchise has been revived at the box office . Meanwhile, I Play Rocky demonstrated major strength as it expanded wide with a rare A+ CinemaScore, and Elsinore notched a promising per-screen average in limited release.

Lionsgate released The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping in 4,018 North American theaters, and the sixth film in the dystopian franchise grossed $120 million in its opening weekend. This gives it the fourth-best debut in franchise history, besting 2015’s second Mockingjay movie ($102.6 million) and 2023 prequel The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes ($44.6 million) but behind 2013’s Catching Fire ($158 million), 2012’s series-launching The Hunger Games ($152.5 million) and 2014’s first Mockingjay ($121.8 million). Its $56 million domestic sum on Friday gave Sunrise the third-best debut Friday in franchise history, behind Catching Fire and The Hunger Games . Related Stories Movies How 'I Play Rocky' Star P.J. Byrne Became One of Hollywood's Go-To Character Actors Beyond the Book "The Secrecy Was Insane:" The Making of 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,' From Locked Safes to Original Cast's Return

The new film added $105 million from 84 international territories for a global haul of $225 million.

Its audience was 67 percent female, with 50 percent of the crowd above age 25, according to PostTrak. Sunrise earned an A- CinemaScore from audiences, putting it below the A grades of the Jennifer Lawrence -led initial 2012 movie that kicked off the series and 2013’s Catching Fire but matching the A- grades of the two Mockingjay films.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will notch the fifth-biggest opening in Lionsgate history, as it also stands at No. 5 among 2026 domestic openings for all studios. It represents the highest-grossing launch for the careers of stars Glenn Close, Jesse Plemons, Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning. This weekend’s haul also brings the Hunger Games franchise’s box office total to roughly $3.437 billion to make it the studio’s highest-grossing franchise ever, topping The Twilight Saga .

Lionsgate had projected The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping to gross north of $80 million , but other sources expected that it would collect between $100 million and $130 million. Adapting author Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel that was published last year, director Francis Lawrence ‘s movie carries a production budget of roughly $150 million as it revitalizes the franchise by telling a story set 24 years before the events of Collins’ original 2008 book.

entertainment.title: Why Ada Brook From The Gilded Age Looks So Familiar
entertainment.summary: If Ada Brook from "The Gilded Age" looks familiar to you, it's probably because the actress who plays her was a mainstay in a long-running HBO franchise.
entertainment.body:
Karolina Wojtasik/HBO Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover If the kind and gentle Ada Brook (now named Ada Forte) on the riveting HBO drama "The Gilded Age" seems familiar to you, it might be because you're a fan of "Sex and the City." Brook is played by Cynthia Nixon, best known for her major role on the '90s HBO dramedy as Miranda Hobbes. Miranda is a career-minded, independent woman who stays in main character Carrie's life throughout the whole series. She played Miranda in the "Sex and the City" movies, and Nixon even returned for the 2021 sequel series "And Just Like That," exploring how Miranda has evolved in middle age.

Away from the "Sex and the City" franchise, you may remember Nixon from an early role in the HBO historical drama movie "Warm Springs," in which she played first lady Eleanor Roosevelt. Other notable small screen roles include Senator Carly Armiston in the Prime Video political satire series "Alpha House," investigator Kade Prurnell in the NBC horror/thriller series "Hannibal," and press secretary Gwendolyn Briggs in Netflix's disappointing "One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest" prequel series "Ratched. " She's also made guest appearances in the likes of "ER," "House," "30 Rock," and "Broad City."

You may also recognize Nixon from the stage. Not only has she starred in many critically acclaimed plays, but in 1984 (when she was still a freshman in college) she became the first Broadway performer to be in two plays at the same time. She would perform the first act of the dark comedy "Hurlyburly," then rush to a different theater for the second act of the drama "The Real Thing," and then return to "Hurlyburly" for the ending. "I only did it for about three months, then gave my notice because I was panicked I would flunk my geology final," she told Playbill .

Nixon leaned into her "Sex and the City" image during her primary run, selling merch labeled "I'm a Miranda and I'm voting for Cynthia." She told Time, "It was a really useful fundraising tool. People know me as Miranda, and I share a lot in common with her. I think it was kind of a shorthand for saying, 'Women like me are stepping up and are outspoken and are warriors and crusaders in the way that Miranda was.'" When asked if she would ever run again, she said, "I don't think I will, but you never know. Life is long and strange."

entertainment.title: 15 TV Shows To Watch If You Like Slow Horses
entertainment.summary: Slow Horses is one of the best spy thrillers on TV these days, and if you're looking for something similar to watch, there are plenty of great options.
entertainment.body:
Apple TV Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover It's a great time to be a fan of spy fiction. If you were keeping up with all the rumors leading up to Robert Pattinson being cast as James Bond, a name you may have heard pop up is Jack Lowden, currently the star of Apple TV's spy thriller "Slow Horses," alongside Gary Oldman, Kristin Scott Thomas, and Olivia Cooke. The series follows a squad of MI5 rejects led by the misanthropic Jackson Lamb (Oldman), who, despite their misfit backgrounds, become involved in unraveling a major counterterrorism plot.

Having just been renewed for Seasons 9 and 10 at Apple TV , "Slow Horses" has slowly but surely emerged as one of the most successful series in the current TV landscape. Though it's far from the only great show of its kind, there's also plenty of series related to "Slow Horses" that you wouldn't necessarily think to check out. Whether you're into the series' gritty espionage tone, its rather unlikely team of antiheroes, or just want to know what other projects its creators have been involved with, these are the 15 shows that should be added to your watchlist while you wait for Season 7 to release.

Fox Before there was "The Pitt," there was "24," a thriller series in which every season also takes place in real time across a 24-hour period. Kiefer Sutherland stars as Jack Bauer, a United States counterterrorism agent, and embodies the exact blend of intelligence and macho necessary for thwarting global catastrophes, including assassinations, nuclear detonations, mass murders, and hostage negotiations. Across nine seasons, accruing nine individual days of Jack's life, "24" changed television forever by making every single episode an event you had to tune in for.

"Slow Horses" is, as the name suggests, a lot slower overall than any given episode of "24." However, it's unlikely that modern-day spy thrillers would be as popular as they are with television audiences if it weren't for shows like "24" turning foreign policy, terrorism, and political friction into something worth watching for entertainment. Sure, Jack Lowden's River might be a far cry skill-wise from the well-rounded Bauer, but "Slow Horses" definitely feels as true to our current worldwide political climate as "24" was for its era.

BBC On the surface, "The Thick of It" doesn't seem at all similar to "Slow Horses." The former is a political comedy focusing the scheming Malcolm Tucker (Peter Capaldi), the fictional director of communications for the British government, and Hugh Abbot (Chris Langham), the inept secretary of state. The reason it shares a lot of DNA with "Slow Horses," however, is because "Slow Horses" creator Will Smith was both a writer on "The Thick of It" and an actor portraying conservative advisor Phil Smith.

entertainment.title: Boy George on His Israel Trip: ‘I Wasn’t Able to Not Say Something’
entertainment.summary: After performing in Tel Aviv and meeting survivors of the Oct. 7 attack, the Culture Club frontman reflects on the backlash to his song, rising antisemitism, and why he felt compelled to speak out
entertainment.body:
“I’ve always joked that I’m a little bit Jew-ish-ish with a big hyphen,” says Culture Club frontman Boy George . He had recently returned from an eight-day trip to Israel, where he performed two sold-out shows at Tel Aviv’s Menora Mivtachim Arena on Nov. 4 and 7. George’s arrival is a rare one, as most Western artists have steered clear of the country, which has been plagued by political infighting, wars in Gaza and Iran, and global criticism for its handling of the conflicts.

But the 65-year-old is defying convention with characteristic flair. George burst on the pop scene in 1982, one of the first MTV stars with the New Wave hit “Do You Really Want to Hurt Me?” Challenging gender and cultural norms in an oversize hat, Rasta dreads, drag makeup, and a T-shirt that spelled Culture Club in Hebrew ( Havurat Aguda ), Boy George was an instant sensation and ruled the pop charts for years to come.

Four decades later, Boy George is still advocating for multiculturalism and LGBTQ+ rights, but his hometown of London feels less tolerant. On his way to the doctor in April, he arrived at the Jewish neighborhood of Golder’s Green moments in the wake of an antisemitic stabbing spree, the culmination of a disturbing 82 percent uptick in physical assaults in the U.K. in the first half of 2026, per the Community Security Trust. He then visited the Nova exhibit in London and released the reggae-infused single “We Will Dance Again” ( Od Nirkod in Hebrew) in late July on Instagram and X. He made his position clear through the lyrics: “You say genocide/I say war…. You condemn the Jews with selective memory/Musicians holding flags, mouthing like sheep…. You never mention Oct. 7/Young girls raped against trees, murdered brutally/For the crime of dancing.”

The song prompted a swift and harsh backlash. He said he “parted ways” with longtime manager of his BGP label, Tony Pontius , was removed from Bandcamp for using AI on the track , lost old friends like Human League and Heaven 17 founder Martyn Ware, was disinvited from a memorial honoring stylist friend Pam Hogg , and was pulled from a West End revival of “Jesus Christ Superstar.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Never one to back down, George spoke out, released his single with live instrumentation on Warner Music/ADA in October (it charted in the U.K. , France, Greece, and Latvia), and announced he would perform in Israel, boycotts be damned. While there, he met with Oct. 7 survivors, victims’ families and held a press conference at the site of the Nova Festival in Re’im, where Hamas killed 378 concertgoers and staff, took 44 hostages, and sexually assaulted concertgoers, according to an independent U.N. investigation.

entertainment.title: Ben McKenzie makes brutal assessment of disgraced crypto Sam Bankman-Fried after one-on-one meeting
entertainment.summary: The actor, who has an economics degree, became interested in cryptocurrency during the COVID-19 pandemic.
entertainment.body:
Ben McKenzie is no fan of convicted fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried, scornfully describing him as “very unimpressive.”

The “O.C.” alum interviewed Bankman-Fried for his 2023 book, “ Easy Money: Cryptocurrency, Casino Capitalism, and the Golden Age of Fraud, ” which he co-wrote with Jacob Silverman, and again for his 2026 documentary, “Everyone is Lying to You for Money.”

McKenzie, 48, told Page Six at the premiere of “The Altruists” that he found the swindler, 34, “very unimpressive, very not charming.”

The actor, who has an economics degree, became interested in cryptocurrency during the COVID-19 pandemic.

“I was bored; a friend was selling me on it,” he explained. “I couldn’t make sense of it. I became sort of obsessed with it, and as I told Congress later, I thought, (it was) perhaps the biggest Ponzi scheme in history.”

McKenzie confessed that he’s slightly shocked by its continued success.

“I watched the last crash in 2022; crypto was left for dead, and then our current president embraced it in the summer of 2024, and crypto is back.”

The “Gotham” actor was on hand at the “Altruists” premiere to moderate the Q&A after the screening.

entertainment.title: Why Lisbeth Anderson From The Body Looks So Familiar
entertainment.summary: The actress who plays Lisbeth Anderson in The Body has played a number of disquieting teen characters. Here's where you may have seen her before.
entertainment.body:
Netflix/YouTube Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover In Netflix's "The Body," Lisbeth Anderson stops at nothing to secure a spot on her Catholic high school's dance team and gain favor with the popular crowd. Played by Geena Meszaros, the eyebrow-less outcast isn't so innocent, as her unnerving family life and ties to a religious cult only amplify the supernatural mystery at the heart of "The Body."

Considering Lisbeth's pivotal role in "The Body," viewers might recognize Meszaros from other projects. After all, the star was featured on a different coming-of-age TV drama before, playing the character Lily on Freevee's "High School" — which was canceled after one season in 2022. The 2025 Netflix thriller miniseries "Wayward" also revolved around disquieting teens, with Meszaros taking on the role of a Tall Pines student named Oatmeal Beth.

When it comes to movies, Meszaros portrayed Bonnie Sue West in 2024's "The Order" — which fittingly centers on the acts of a heinous cult. Those who saw the 2025 Maika Monroe-led psychological crime thriller "In Cold Light" might recall Meszaros' appearance as the older version of Amy.

Netflix/YouTube "The Body" places Geena Meszaros in the shoes of an off-putting newcomer who has more of a talent for conning than dancing. Eager to weaponize her peers' secrets for her own gain, Lisbeth grows close to the vulnerable Anya (Kristina Bogic) after helping her deal with Grace's (Sofia Wylie) then-presumed-dead body on Halloween. Later taking advantage of Maddie's (Shirley Chen) eating disorder and viciously butting heads with the more clear-eyed Elise (Sara Boustany), Lisbeth navigates several complex relationships outside of her troubled family.

Being raised in a religious cult influences Lisbeth as she blackmails and manipulates her way onto the dance squad, but according to Meszaros, the character's actions have nothing to do with faith. "She was deeply religious, but then that was fully stripped away from her," the actress told Elite Daily . "So she's in a very anti-religion moment. She's like, 'Oh, nobody's looking out for me except for me.' And that's the core of all the choices that she makes."

Should Netflix greenlight "The Body" Season 2, Lisbeth looks poised for a fascinating next chapter after successfully pushing the lie that she resurrected Grace and uncovering another skeleton in Anya's closet. Shows as mysterious and thrilling as "The Body" rarely show all their cards at once. Thus, a potential second season should reveal a lot more about Lisbeth.
